data.about: Six floor plans, each with a few walls in it, and one question: does the slab stay put? A wall can only take a force along its own axis, so each wall is one force on one known line. Three lines against the three freedoms of a body in plane — two slides and a spin — and the whole of task 1 is the rule that follows: the axes must be neither all parallel nor all concurrent. Five of the six panels answer themselves. Panel e) does not: its three axes meet at a point eight tenths of a panel-width off the right edge, invisible unless you extend them, and that is why it fails. Drag a wall and watch the verdict flip.

steps.caption: EX 10 task 1: six layouts of bracing walls in a floor plan, and a tick box under each. The sheet gives no scale and no load direction — so the answer cannot depend on either, and the whole task is one geometric rule
steps.title: The exercise

steps.caption: right: all six, drawn as the sheet draws them — walls as thick rectangles, nothing dimensioned. Panels a) and f) put their walls on the edges, b) makes a closed core, c) d) and e) put them across the middle
steps.title: The six layouts

steps.caption: left: panel e), big enough to work on. Choose another in the panel, and drag any wall by its handle — the verdict recomputes as you move it
steps.title: One panel, enlarged

steps.caption: every wall centreline, run right across the plan and well past its edges. This is the step the sheet asks for and the step students skip: an axis does not stop where the concrete stops
steps.title: Extend the axes

steps.caption: every axis of panel e) passes through ONE point. The slab can still rotate about it — the walls simply swing round the pole and never stretch, so they never resist. Not braced
steps.title: They all meet — it does not hold

steps.caption: the same axes drawn into every thumbnail. Read them off: are they all parallel? do they all meet at one point? Nothing else matters
steps.title: Now all six

steps.caption: three of the six tick. a) has too few walls, c) has two collinear ones so it has too few axes, and e) has three good axes that happen to be concurrent — the only one of the three failures you cannot see without extending the lines
steps.title: The answer key
